feel: verb
experience a physical feeling or emotion
typical: feel + adjective: tired, hungry, happy, fine, sad. NOT for: touching with hands.
I feel tired after the trip.
Do you still feel hungry?
verb
give a particular impression when touched or experienced
typical: thing + feel + adjective/like. NOT for: people's emotions.
This fabric feels soft.
The room felt cold and empty.
verb
have an opinion or belief
typical: feel that + clause, feel strongly. NOT for: physical sensations.
I feel that we should wait.
Many parents feel strongly about this.
verb
want to do something
typical: feel like + -ing, feel like + noun. NOT for: emotions in general.
I don't feel like going out tonight.
Do you feel like a coffee?
verb
touch something to learn about it
typical: feel + object (with your hands). NOT for: emotions.
Feel this fabric.
She felt his forehead to see if he was hot.
verb
(spoken) feel free: used to say that someone is welcome to do something
typical: feel free to + verb. NOT for: emotions.
Feel free to ask me anything.
Please feel free to sit down.
face off: fight, argue or compete with someone (AmE)
typical: face off against/with sb. NOT for: cooperating.
The candidates will face off in a debate.
The two teams face off on Friday.
face up to: accept and deal with a difficult fact or problem
typical: face up to the truth/a problem/reality. NOT for: avoiding.
You must face up to the fact he's guilty.
She had to face up to her mistakes.
fade away: typical: hopes/memories/sounds fade away. NOT for: growing stronger.
Hopes of a peace settlement began to fade away.
become weaker physically, especially so that you become very ill or die
typical: sb fades away. NOT for: recovering.
The old man faded away in his last months.
She watched her mother fade away.
fade out: typical: a sound/picture fades out. NOT for: growing louder.
The song fades out at the end.
make a sound or picture slowly disappear
typical: fade sth out. NOT for: fading it in.
The editor faded out the scene.
fall apart: verb
stop being effective or successful (a plan, relationship or system)
typical: plans/a marriage falls apart. NOT for: working well.
Their plans fell apart.
The health service is falling apart.
verb
be in very bad condition
typical: be falling apart. NOT for: being new.
His old bike was falling apart.
The house is falling apart.
verb
break into pieces
typical: fall apart in your hands. NOT for: staying whole.
The book fell apart in my hands.
The cake fell apart.
verb
be unable to deal with problems emotionally
typical: fall apart (after sth). NOT for: coping.
She fell apart after the divorce.
Don't fall apart now.
verb
suffer something very bad and serious that changes your life completely
typical: sb's world/life falls apart. NOT for: things improving.
Her whole world fell apart when her husband died.
His life fell apart after the accident.
fall back on: use something or depend on someone when other things fail
typical: have sb/sth to fall back on. NOT for: depending first.
She has no relatives to fall back on.
They fell back on the law.
fall behind: go more slowly than others so that they get ahead
typical: fall behind (sb). NOT for: catching up.
She hurt her ankle and fell behind the others.
He fell behind in the race.
typical: fall behind (sb/sth) in sth. NOT for: making progress.
Companies that don't change fall behind.
not do something by the time you should
typical: fall behind with payments/work. NOT for: paying on time.
He fell behind with the rent.
fall down: fall to the ground from standing
typical: fall down the stairs/in the street. NOT for: stay standing.
The child fell down and cried.
be in very bad condition (a building)
typical: be falling down. NOT for: being repaired.
The old barn is falling down.
fail because of a particular reason or in a particular way
typical: fall down on sth, that's where it falls down. NOT for: succeeding.
That's where the argument falls down.
He is falling down on the job.
fall for: be tricked into believing something false (informal)
typical: fall for a trick/story/lie. NOT for: seeing through.
He's too smart to fall for that trick.
typical: fall for sb. NOT for: falling out of love.
She fell for Lucy at the fairground.
He fell for her at once.
like a place or thing immediately
typical: fall for sth. NOT for: disliking.
I fell for the town at once.
fall in: typical: the roof falls in. NOT for: standing.
The ceiling fell in during the storm.
start walking in a line behind someone
typical: fall in (behind sb). NOT for: falling out.
His men fell in behind him.
fall off: verb
become separated from the main part
typical: a handle/button falls off. NOT for: staying attached.
The door handle keeps falling off.
A button fell off her jacket.
verb
decrease in amount, rate or quality
typical: sales/numbers fall off. NOT for: rising.
Audience figures fell off.
Sales fell off in winter.
verb
fall down from something such as a bike or horse
typical: fall off a bike/chair/wall. NOT for: getting on.
He fell off his bike.
The child fell off the wall.
verb
be very surprised (spoken)
typical: nearly/almost fall off your chair. NOT for: being bored.
I nearly fell off my chair when I saw my brother on stage.
She almost fell off her chair at the news.
fall out: typical: fall out with sb (over sth). NOT for: making up.
Carrie's always falling out with people.
no longer be attached (a tooth or hair)
typical: hair/a tooth falls out. NOT for: growing.
The drug made her hair fall out.
stop standing in line and move away (soldiers)
typical: fall out. NOT for: falling in.
fall over: fall onto the ground from an upright position
typical: fall over, fall over sth. NOT for: staying up.
Tommy fell over and cut his knee.
hit your foot on something and fall (fall over sth)
typical: fall over the dog/a step. NOT for: walking safely.
be very eager to do something (fall over yourself)
typical: fall over yourself to do sth. NOT for: ignoring.
People fell over themselves to help.
He fell over himself to please her.
fall through: not be completed successfully (a plan, sale or agreement)
typical: a deal/plan falls through. NOT for: going ahead.
feel like: want to do or have something
typical: feel like + -ing/noun, I don't feel like it. NOT for: being sure.
I don't feel like going out tonight.
Do you feel like a coffee?
seem similar to something when touched or experienced
typical: feel like + noun. NOT for: wanting something.
feel up to: have the strength or energy to do something (usually in questions or negatives)
typical: feel up to doing sth, don't feel up to it. NOT for: wanting.
I just didn't feel up to going.
Do you feel up to a walk?
fend off: defend yourself against someone attacking you
typical: fend sb off. NOT for: attacking.
She fended her attacker off with her arm.
avoid something difficult (questions, competition or a takeover)
typical: fend off questions/criticism/a bid. NOT for: welcoming.
She uses her secretary to fend off calls.
The firm fended off a takeover bid.
fight back: work hard to oppose something, especially when losing
typical: fight back (against sth). NOT for: giving up.
She fought back against the cancer.
use violence or arguments against someone who attacked you
typical: fight back. NOT for: surrendering.
If he hits you, fight back.
try hard not to show a feeling
typical: fight back tears/anger. NOT for: showing feelings.
fight off: defend yourself successfully against an attack
typical: fight sb/sth off. NOT for: giving in.
successfully resist an illness or a feeling
typical: fight off a cold/sleep/an infection. NOT for: catching an illness.
figure out: find the answer to a problem by thinking
typical: figure sth out, figure out how/what/why. NOT for: being told the answer.
Can you figure out how to do it?
understand why someone behaves in a certain way
typical: figure sb out. NOT for: knowing someone.
I just can't figure her out.
file away: put documents into a file or storage place
typical: file sth away. NOT for: taking out.
fill in: verb
write information on a form or document
typical: fill in a form/card/name. NOT for: reading it.
Fill in your boarding card.
Please fill in the form.
verb
tell someone about recent events
typical: fill sb in (on sth). NOT for: hiding things.
Fill me in on what's happened.
I'll fill you in later.
verb
fill a hole or space so it is level
typical: fill sth in. NOT for: digging.
They filled in the hole.
Fill in the cracks with paste.
verb
do a job for someone for a short time (fill in for sb)
typical: fill in (for sb). NOT for: a permanent job.
I'm filling in for Sam today.
He filled in while she was away.
verb
use time while waiting
typical: fill in time/an hour. NOT for: wasting a day.
I filled in an hour reading.
We filled in time at a café.
verb
colour or paint the space inside a shape or outline
typical: fill sth in. NOT for: leaving blank.
The children filled in the pictures with crayons.
She filled in the letters with red ink.
fill in for: do someone's job for a short time while they are away
typical: fill in for sb. NOT for: replacing permanently.
I'm filling in for Sam today.
She filled in for the teacher.
fill out: verb
write all the information needed on a form
typical: fill out a form/an application. NOT for: reading.
Please fill out this form.
He filled out the application.
verb
become slightly fatter (adult or young body)
typical: fill out, a body fills out. NOT for: losing weight.
Eric has filled out around the waist.
Her body began to fill out.
verb
grow into an adult-looking body (a young person)
typical: a young person's body fills out. NOT for: staying childlike.
At puberty, a girl's body begins to fill out.
He has started to fill out and look like a man.
verb
add more details to make something complete
typical: fill sth out. NOT for: cutting things.
Fill out the report with some data.
He filled out his story.
fill up: become full, or make a container full
typical: fill up (with sth), fill sth up. NOT for: emptying.
Her eyes filled up with tears.
Shall I fill the car up?
eat so much that you cannot eat more (informal)
typical: fill yourself up with/on sth. NOT for: feeling hungry.
make you feel you have eaten a lot (food)
typical: food fills you up. NOT for: hunger.
The soup really filled me up.
find out: get information by looking for it or by chance
typical: find out what/how/if/that, find out about sth. NOT for: looking for a lost object.
Did you find out how much it costs?
I need to find out more about the course.
discover that someone has done something dishonest or illegal
typical: get found out, find sb out. NOT for: discovering facts.
What happens if we get found out?
He was found out after a week.
find out about: discover facts about someone or something
typical: find out about sb/sth. NOT for: knowing already.
I need to find out about the course.
She found out about the plan.
finish off: verb
complete the last part of something
typical: finish sth off. NOT for: starting.
It'll take me two hours to finish this off.
She finished off the report.
verb
use or eat all of something
typical: finish sth off (the cake). NOT for: leaving some.
Who finished off the cake?
He finished off the bottle.
verb
complete an event or performance with a final action
typical: finish off with sth. NOT for: beginning.
We'll finish off with a new song.
They finished off with a toast.
verb
kill or defeat someone completely (informal)
typical: finish sb off. NOT for: helping.
The blow finished him off.
The last attack finished off the enemy.
finish up: be in a place or situation in the end (BrE informal)
typical: finish up in/as/doing sth. NOT for: planned trips.
eat or use all of something
typical: finish up your dinner. NOT for: wasting.
Finish up and go to bed.
fire up: make someone very excited, interested or angry
typical: be fired up (about sth). NOT for: calming.
She got fired up about small things.
The coach fired up the team.
typical: fire up a computer/engine/grill. NOT for: switching off.
fit in: verb
be accepted by a group
typical: fit in (with sb), fit in at school. NOT for: standing out.
I never really fitted in at school.
She fits in well with the team.
verb
manage to do or see someone despite being busy
typical: fit sb/sth in. NOT for: cancelling.
The doctor can fit me in at 4:30.
I wanted to fit in a swim.
verb
be small enough to go into a space
typical: fit in the car/box. NOT for: not fitting.
Will it all fit in the car?
The bag won't fit in the locker.
verb
match or be suitable for a plan or situation
typical: fit in with sth. NOT for: contradicting.
Does that fit in with your plans?
The idea fits in well.
fix up: verb
arrange a meeting or an event
typical: fix sth up, fix up a time/interview. NOT for: cancelling.
I fixed up an interview with him.
We'll fix up a time.
verb
decorate or repair a room or building
typical: fix up a room/house. NOT for: wrecking.
We fixed up the guest room.
He fixed up an old house.
verb
provide someone with something they need
typical: fix sb up with sth. NOT for: taking away.
Can you fix me up with a bed for the night?
She fixed him up with a job.
verb
find a romantic partner for someone
typical: fix sb up with sb. NOT for: avoiding matchmaking.
My friend fixed me up with a date.
They fixed her up with a colleague.
flare up: suddenly start burning more strongly, or start again (fire or illness)
typical: a fire/illness/pain flares up. NOT for: dying down.
His back pain flared up again.
suddenly become angry or violent (a situation)
typical: violence/anger/tempers flare up. NOT for: calming.
Tempers flared up at the meeting.
suddenly become worse (a disease or injury)
typical: an illness/injury flares up. NOT for: recovering.
His old knee injury flared up again.
The skin disease flares up in winter.
flip out: suddenly become very angry or upset, or lose control (informal)
typical: flip out about/over sth. NOT for: staying calm.
She flipped out when she saw the mess.
He flipped out over the news.
follow up: find out more about something and take action if necessary
typical: follow sth up, a follow-up. NOT for: ignoring.
do something extra to make something more successful
typical: follow sth up with sth. NOT for: stopping.
Follow up your email with a phone call.
The test was followed up by others.
fool around: verb
waste time behaving in a silly way
typical: fool around (in class). NOT for: working.
He fooled around in class.
Stop fooling around!
verb
behave carelessly or dangerously with something
typical: fool around with sth. NOT for: being careful.
Someone's been fooling around with the wires.
Don't fool around with fire.
verb
spend time doing something you enjoy that has no particular purpose (AmE)
typical: just fool around (in the yard). NOT for: working seriously.
The boys were out in the yard, just fooling around.
We fooled around on the beach all day.
verb
have casual romantic or sexual relationships (informal)
typical: fool around with sb. NOT for: being faithful.
He was fooling around with another woman.
They fooled around at university.
freak out: become very anxious, upset or afraid, or make someone so (informal)
typical: freak out, freak sb out. NOT for: staying calm.
People freaked out at the news.
The whole idea freaked me out.
freeze up: become solid with cold so that it stops working (a pipe or engine)
typical: pipes/an engine freeze up. NOT for: thawing.
suddenly be unable to speak or act
typical: freeze up (on stage). NOT for: speaking easily.
He froze up in the interview.
